name: Stimulant use disorder (cocaine, methamphetamine, other stimulants)

icd11.label: Harmful pattern of use of cocaine
Harmful pattern of use of stimulants including amphetamines, methamphetamine or methcathinone
Stimulant dependence including amphetamines, methamphetamine or methcathinone

dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders — Stimulant Use Disorder
summary: A pattern, described in ICD-11 terms, in which use of cocaine, methamphetamine or misused prescription stimulants slips out of the client's control, often in binges, and takes priority over health, money, work and relationships, with intense craving and a crash of exhaustion and low mood after use. Stimulants can cause chest pain, heart rhythm problems, stroke, paranoia and psychosis, and the drug supply may contain fentanyl. Contingency management has the strongest evidence; there is no approved medication, so medical care for complications and harm reduction matter. Substance-use information is protected: nothing here is stored or sent, and every export carries the Part 2 notice. 42 CFR Part 2 prohibits unauthorized use or disclosure of these records. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask about the pattern of use over the past year, including binges and attempts to stop. DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 both look at the pattern over months; check the timing they describe.

ruleOuts.label: Opioid exposure through the drug supply
ruleOuts.note: Fentanyl contamination raises overdose risk; offer naloxone. This app does not store or send substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Heart, stroke and other medical complications
ruleOuts.note: Chest pain, palpitations, severe headache or weakness need emergency care.

ruleOuts.label: Primary psychotic, bipolar or ADHD conditions
ruleOuts.note: Ask whether paranoia, highs or attention problems occur during sober periods.

specifiers.label: ICD-10-CM coding notes
specifiers.note: F14.x codes cocaine and F15.x codes other stimulants (amphetamine-type); .1x is a harmful (abuse) pattern and .2x a dependence pattern. DSM-5-TR uses its own severity and course specifiers: See DSM-5-TR.

differentials.label: Stimulant-induced psychotic disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Paranoia or hallucinations during heavy use that clear with abstinence.

differentials.label: Adult ADHD with prescribed stimulant treatment
differentials.distinguishing: Prescribed use as directed without loss of control or harm.

comorbidities.label: Depression
comorbidities.note: Crash-related low mood is common; screen with the PHQ-9 and ask about suicide.

comorbidities.label: Psychosis
comorbidities.note: Stimulants can trigger psychosis; assess during sober periods.

comorbidities.label: Adult ADHD
comorbidities.note: Untreated ADHD is a risk factor; coordinate any stimulant prescribing carefully.

interventions.name: Contingency management (first line)
interventions.evidence: A network meta-analysis (De Crescenzo et al., 2018) found contingency management, alone or with community reinforcement, the most effective psychosocial treatment for cocaine and amphetamine addiction.
interventions.note: Refer to programs that offer it.

interventions.name: CBT and community reinforcement
interventions.evidence: Supported in the same network meta-analysis (De Crescenzo et al., 2018).
interventions.note: Coping skills, activity planning and support networks.

interventions.name: Naloxone and harm reduction
interventions.evidence: The drug supply may contain fentanyl; take-home naloxone reduces deaths (McDonald and Strang, 2016).
interventions.note: Offer naloxone, fentanyl test strips where legal, and never-use-alone planning.

interventions.name: Medical care for complications
interventions.evidence: Stimulants carry cardiovascular and psychiatric risks.

culturalNotes: Norms about cannabis, prescription pills and other drugs vary widely, and legal status differs by state and country. Anchor the assessment in control and harm, not in legal status or amounts alone.

Stigma, fear of losing custody, housing, work or immigration status, and past experiences with police can make clients cautious. Explain confidentiality, its limits and 42 CFR Part 2 protections plainly.
Use person-first, non-judgmental language (a person who uses drugs, not an addict) and offer harm-reduction options alongside abstinence goals.
Culturally grounded and community-led programs, including Indigenous healing approaches and peer recovery services, are often more acceptable; ask what support looks like for the client.

Faith can be a strong support in recovery. Offer faith-based groups or faith-integrated approaches only when the client asks and after informed consent (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors).
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.

redFlagRules.message: Suicide-related content is documented in this input. Substance use raises suicide risk, especially during intoxication, withdrawal or after a loss; ask directly, include substances and other means in safety planning, and follow your risk protocol.
Psychotic symptoms are documented. Stimulant-induced psychosis needs urgent medical and psychiatric evaluation; check for risk to self or others.

Possible overdose, intoxication or medication toxicity is documented. Call emergency services if the person is hard to wake or breathing poorly, give naloxone if opioids may be involved, and arrange same-day medical care.
